subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm planning a full module for a Genshin Impact-style toon kit: cel shading, fur edges, anime eyes, ink outlines, featuring a red panda balanced on a mossy stone with ornamental Genshin-style touches like elemental swirls, glowing runes, and a floating dendro seed with leaves.

I'm working out the pose — a quadruped stance on a flat-topped boulder with the tail curled for balance — then sketching rough scale (panda body ~0.55m, stone ~0.5m wide) and sketching out the skeleton hierarchy from hips through spine to neck and head, placing joint coordinates to build the rig.

Then a head joint off the neck, aiming toward where the head center should be. I'm reconsidering the bone-list approach for the body loft, thinking I should bind it across the spine chain plus tail rather than complicating things with multiple chain sweeps.

Simplifying further, I'll just go with a loft body using bone list [hips, spine], keeping skinning smooth by default since that's less risky, and treat the tail as a separate chain from the body path entirely.

For the neck, since red pandas have short, thick necks, I'll make it a short rigid sweep attached to a single neck bone plus head joint, sitting right in front of the chest. Now I'm working out the front leg placement—shoulders near the upper chest sides, feet below, with upper and lower leg segments roughly matching in length to span the distance to the ground.

For hind legs I'm sketching a three-segment chain with alternating forward/backward bends to reach the foot target, accounting for the stone surface height and paw pad thickness so the paws sit just above it with slight sinking. I'm naming the limb chain joints now, starting with shoulder and elbow.

For the limb sweep geometry, I'm defining radius tapering from upper leg to paw and using dark brown/black coloring for legs, matching red panda anatomy. I'm settling on a Genshin-style palette: saturated orange-red fur, cream undertones, and dark purplish-black for the legs.

For the tail, I'm working out ringed coloring with alternating orange and dark red-brown bands, implementing this through a custom paint function that checks position along the tail axis to decide which color band applies, wrapped inside the cel-shading logic so lit and shadow versions both get the ring pattern correctly.

Now I'm plotting the tail's curve as a chain of points sweeping up and back from the hips in an S-shape for balance, sizing it bushier and a bit longer than real red pandas for a stylized look, and setting overall proportions like head height for the whole figure.

Adding fur tuft cards along the tail and cheek ruffs for extra fluff detail, tinted orange and scattered at low density.

Now I'm shaping the red panda head itself: a wide rounded skull with short snout, large triangular ears with white inner edges, white cheek ruffs and muzzle, dark nose, and reddish-brown tear-streak marks running from eyes to mouth, all built chibi-style with an oversized head sphere positioned and scaled around the head center, with face paint split between orange on top and cream on the lower muzzle/cheeks using position-based shading relative to that center.

For the eyes, I'm going anime-style big and cute despite real red pandas having small dark eyes, choosing a green iris to contrast nicely against the orange fur rather than a dendro-matching amber tone.

I'll skip the brow decal since I'm painting white brow patches separately instead, but keep the pink blush on the cream cheeks for cuteness. For eye placement, I'm positioning the decal on the skull sphere using the head's half-width to scale size appropriately, mirroring left/right sides, and matching the example's lash-flick detail at the outer corner.

For the cheek ruffs, I'm extruding three overlapping leaf-shaped cream blades per side, angled outward-back with thin thickness. For the ears, I'm shaping a rounded triangular outline with smoothing, orange outside and cream inner edge, extruded and tilted to sit atop the skull.

Working out the orthogonal basis for a 25° outward tilt plus forward lean so the ear's thickness axis stays perpendicular to its outline. I'll wrap this into an earOrient helper, then plan the inner ear as a smaller cream extrusion set slightly in front, with white fur edges against the orange outer ear typical of a red panda.

For the muzzle I'm planning a small cream sphere scaled forward with a dark rounded nose tip, plus a separate lower jaw joint parented to the head so the mouth can open -- a tiny cream ellipsoid wedge beneath the muzzle, skipping tongue or fangs but considering a simple ink line for the smile.

I'm deciding to add that smile as a decal on the muzzle surface -- a tiny "ω"-shaped mouth drawn below the nose, oriented facing forward on the sphere. For the head joint, I'm working out the local direction vectors (forward, up, left/right) following the documented convention for positioning joints relative to their parent.

I'm thinking it's cleaner to define positions in explicit model-space coordinates via a small helper function around fixed head-center constants, rather than relying purely on local direction words, and to pass the bone explicitly for any part or decal attached near the head to avoid ambiguity about which joint it binds to.

Now I'm laying out the body loft stations with coordinates and widths/heights at each torso height, working out where the body bottom sits so I can figure out the leg length needed to reach the ground.

Setting paw target y to 0.29 so the foot nestles just into the stone top, with a flat mossy cap sitting at that stone thickness and tufts decorating the edges rather than under the paws. Now I'm working out the body station coordinates with the center at y=0.58.

I'm defining five loft stations from rump to shoulder with their z positions, y heights, and width/height dimensions, then considering how the loft function handles end caps and cross-section shape -- likely elliptical by default. For coloring, I'm planning a countershade scheme typical of red pandas: orange across the back transitioning to dark brown-black on the belly and legs, using a cel-shaded approach based on the normal's y component.

I'm wrapping a zigzag fur-edge pattern between orange and dark colors along the belly line with cel shading applied on top, then working out the spine and hip joint chain -- placing hip roots and spine control points so that a three-point catmull spline yields two named spine joints, with the second spine joint serving as the chest.

Now I'm defining the neck chain as a two-point polyline producing a single "neck" joint parented to the last spine joint, then setting up the head joint with its aim direction, parent, and skull sphere scale.

I'm considering whether a connecting neck capsule is needed so the head doesn't appear to float, since the chest geometry already extends close to where the skull begins.

I also want to think about the red panda's facial markings—white fur with reddish-brown tear-mark stripes—to make the head read correctly against the body coloring.

I'll add dark red tear stripe decals below each eye, size the eyes and position them using angular coordinates around the skull, and place small cream eyebrow spots above them on the orange cap region.

For the muzzle, I'm using a scaled cream sphere positioned just in front of center, with a smaller dark nose sphere placed just ahead of the muzzle surface, working out the exact z-offsets so the nose sits flush against the muzzle front.

For the jaw, I'm adding an upper muzzle piece and a lower jaw ellipsoid attached at the jaw joint, keeping the mouth closed without needing a separate dark interior piece, possibly adding a subtle mouth line as a decal detail.

Writing blade geometry...

Now I'm sketching the ears: positioned on either side of the head with outward tilt, cream-orange outer shape with a smaller inner cream patch offset forward, plus a small white fringe tuft at the rim. For the body I'm deciding against a distinct chest bib, keeping things simple.

I'm also adding toon-style two-tone shading for both the stone and moss, plus scattering a few smaller rock chunks and a mossy cap around the boulder for visual variety.
